observations.statement: GRS-009 separates worker, planner, evaluator, reducer, verifier, adjudicator, and runtime-controller roles; worker output remains a proposal until a stronger or deterministic layer acts, and workers cannot certify global or parent completion.

Material claims must carry source_spans, target_spans, and evidence_refs; no-material claims must carry no_material_items_found, source_span_checked, and one of the named disposition reasons, while no-op or low-change completion claims require coverage evidence.

GRS-010 requires persistent, separate model-role policy, conditional verifier/adjudicator inheritance, provider-neutral support for lower-quality model paths, and blocking behavior for strong-certification goals whose verifier/adjudicator requirement is unmet.

GRS-011 enumerates evidence, conflict, retry, certification-surface, destructive/governance, confidence, density, target-change, test, scope, validator, and unsupported-claim conditions that route to stronger review independently of provider-specific names.

Every goal must produce a completion receipt or a stopped, blocked, or degraded receipt; completion authority belongs to the runtime controller/evaluator/certifier, and receipts separate source, canonical, process, governance, unresolved-item, changed-artifact, and validator evidence.

Goal completion requires input inventory, work representation or disposition, validation disposition, satisfied acceptance criteria, explicit unresolved items, and complete source/target accounting; Ledger-to-Plans completion adds live-Plan representation or explicit unresolved disposition, conflict preservation, absence of unsupported inventions, and source-to-target evidence.

GRS-013 defines lightweight, standard, and strong-certification evidence profiles and requires mutation, migration, destructive, and governance-sensitive goals to use stronger certification than read-only goals.

When a verifier/adjudicator is unavailable, low-risk goals may finish degraded, standard goals may degrade only under the stated mutation/check condition, and strong-certification goals block; receipts retain the enumerated evidence while raw logs are capped, redacted, stored separately, and referenced.

The core declares a dependency chain from GRS-009 through GRS-014: GRS-009 depends on GRS-006; GRS-010 on GRS-009; GRS-011 on GRS-009 and GRS-010; GRS-012 on GRS-009 and GRS-011; GRS-013 on GRS-012; and GRS-014 on GRS-013.

Every core unit is explicitly classified gui_related false, with its behavior assigned to backend, control-plane, runtime, validation, governance, or evidence policy rather than direct GUI implementation.
Every core unit explicitly sets create_worknodes to false in its node_compile_hint.
The named validation surfaces pair the generic plan-index validator with future unit-specific policy, receipt, or retention tests rather than present runtime test definitions.

Implementation and ownership references connect the runtime policies to future Goal Mode and provider-policy layers, Settings storage and model/account plans, runtime evidence storage, the Runtime Artifacts Panel, and storage-plan; Project_Output_Artifacts is explicitly only a boundary reference and does not own Goal Runtime receipts.

candidate_findings.title: Worker claim payloads lack a complete validation contract
candidate_findings.statement: GRS-009 names mandatory material and no-material fields and disposition tokens, but the core does not define record schemas, field types, cardinality, span coordinate rules, evidence-reference resolution, or validation behavior for malformed or contradictory claims.
candidate_findings.impact: Independent workers and verifiers can serialize or interpret nominally identical claims differently, weakening coverage proof and the prohibition on unsupported content becoming canonical or completion evidence.

candidate_findings.title: Verifier qualification is not machine-decidable
candidate_findings.statement: GRS-010 requires an inherited or selected verifier/adjudicator model to satisfy a required policy and blocks underqualified strong-certification execution, but it does not define the capability attributes, comparison rule, policy authority/version, or evidence that proves qualification.
candidate_findings.impact: The required strong-certification block cannot be implemented or independently verified consistently, so builders can make consequentially different model-qualification decisions.

candidate_findings.title: Task type is omitted from the role-policy acceptance record
candidate_findings.statement: The canonical model-role policy lists task type as an escalation input, while the acceptance criterion that enumerates preserved role-policy fields includes risk_class, failure_count, and provider constraints but omits task type; no stable field spelling or type is supplied.
candidate_findings.impact: A validator can accept a role-policy record that cannot reproduce a required escalation input, causing policy drift between the normative sentence and its acceptance oracle.

candidate_findings.title: Certification tier vocabulary and assignment are underdefined
candidate_findings.statement: The core alternates among low-risk, lightweight read-only or answer-only, standard, and strong-certification terms and says mutation-sensitive work uses stronger certification, but it does not explicitly equate the vocabularies or define a deterministic tier-assignment authority and rule for mixed-risk or phase-changing goals.
candidate_findings.impact: The same goal can receive different verifier inheritance, evidence, degraded-mode, and blocking behavior depending on builder interpretation, including under-certification of mutation or governance work.

candidate_findings.title: Escalation trigger predicates are qualitative
candidate_findings.statement: GRS-011 requires escalation for stale or non-replayable evidence, repeated retries or blockers, low confidence, high-density slices, high-signal empty or weak results, large deletion or replacement, and unsupported claims, but supplies no thresholds, measurement fields, evaluation timing, or deterministic predicate definitions.
candidate_findings.impact: Equivalent runs can fire materially different safety paths, and false negatives can allow unsupported completion while false positives can cause unnecessary review or blocking.

candidate_findings.title: Escalation destination, precedence, and termination are unspecified
candidate_findings.statement: The policy offers stronger verifier, second-pass worker, adjudicator, or stronger policy handling as destinations but does not map triggers to destinations, define precedence when multiple triggers fire, specify who selects the route, or state a terminal fallback when escalation cannot resolve the condition.
candidate_findings.impact: Implementations can diverge in authority and safety, produce escalation loops, or prematurely certify after an unresolved trigger.

candidate_findings.title: Out-of-scope-write escalation does not preserve the authority boundary explicitly
candidate_findings.statement: Out-of-scope writes are defined as an escalation trigger and must not be ignored, but the core does not state whether the write must be rejected, rolled back, quarantined, or merely reviewed, nor does it state that escalation cannot grant the missing write authority.
candidate_findings.impact: A handler could treat escalation as authorization for an otherwise forbidden mutation, leaving unsafe or unauthorized artifacts in place.

candidate_findings.title: Completion decision authority is plural but unresolved
candidate_findings.statement: GRS-012 says the controller/evaluator/certifier decides completion and distinguishes those decisions from worker claims, but it does not define whether these are aliases, ordered stages, separate authorities, a quorum, or how conflicting decisions are adjudicated.
candidate_findings.impact: Two conforming implementations can produce opposite completion states from the same evidence, and no deterministic final authority exists within the core.

candidate_findings.title: Completion receipt schema and lifecycle are incomplete
candidate_findings.statement: The core enumerates receipt evidence and stopped, blocked, degraded, and complete outcomes, but it does not define a typed receipt schema, goal/attempt identity, status enum, timestamps, policy version, immutable versus amendable fields, atomic commit with goal state, supersession after reopen, or failure behavior when receipt persistence fails.
candidate_findings.impact: Receipts may be non-interoperable, non-replayable, duplicated, or inconsistent with the runtime state they are intended to certify.

candidate_findings.title: Validation skipping lacks authorization and admissibility rules
candidate_findings.statement: Required validations may be explicitly skipped with reason and standard checks may be run or skipped with reason, but the core does not define who can authorize a skip, acceptable reason classes, which checks are unskippable, or how a skipped required check changes certification tier or status.
candidate_findings.impact: A free-form skip reason can become a path around required evidence and allow a normal completion receipt without a meaningful validation oracle.

candidate_findings.title: Completeness and source-to-target mapping lack an operational oracle
candidate_findings.statement: The policy requires coverage evidence, inventoried inputs, represented or dispositioned work, no unaccounted source or target areas, material-ledger coverage, and source-to-target mapping where applicable, but it does not define materiality, valid disposition kinds, mapping schema/cardinality, or an algorithm for proving exhaustive accounting.
candidate_findings.impact: A receipt can assert complete coverage without a reproducible way for the verifier to detect omitted source material or target areas.

candidate_findings.title: Independent verification semantics are ambiguous
candidate_findings.statement: Strong certification requires an independent verifier or verifier role, while model inheritance is conditionally allowed, but the core does not define independence across agent identity, conversation/session, model instance, provider/account, evidence construction, or organizational authority.
candidate_findings.impact: A worker can potentially self-verify by changing roles, satisfying the wording without providing the independent challenge that strong certification is intended to require.

candidate_findings.title: Degraded completion state transitions are not fully specified
candidate_findings.statement: The core permits low-risk degraded finish, conditionally permits standard degradation, blocks strong-certification goals, and requires stopped, blocked, or degraded receipts, but it does not define whether degraded is terminal completion, what no mutation or required check is affected means, who proves that condition, or how blocked/degraded goals resume and later supersede their receipts.
candidate_findings.impact: Status handling and user-visible completion truth can diverge, with some runtimes treating degraded as done and others as pending or failed.

candidate_findings.title: Log redaction and evidence retention controls are not implementable from the core
candidate_findings.statement: Raw logs must be capped, redacted, separately stored, and hash/path referenced, and secrets must not be retained, but the core does not set cap/truncation semantics, sensitive-data classes or redaction verification, hash algorithm, path durability, access controls, encryption, retention duration, deletion policy, or behavior when separate storage fails.
candidate_findings.impact: Builders can leak secrets, lose replay evidence, retain sensitive data indefinitely, or issue receipts whose referenced logs cannot be retrieved or integrity-checked consistently.

candidate_findings.title: Runtime acceptance oracles remain placeholders
candidate_findings.statement: Each unit names the generic plan-index validator and a future unit-specific test surface, but the assigned core provides no executable runtime test vectors, fixtures, expected state transitions, or pass/fail assertions for role policy, escalation, receipt certification, degraded mode, or redaction.
candidate_findings.impact: The accepted requirements cannot yet be certified behaviorally, and structurally valid plan metadata may be mistaken for proof that runtime safety behavior works.

candidate_findings.title: Ordering, concurrency, and idempotency are unspecified
candidate_findings.statement: The core defines proposal, verification, routing, completion decisions, and receipt creation, but does not define ordering among those stages, deduplication of repeated claims or child receipts, idempotent retry keys, concurrency control, or resolution of competing receipt writes.
candidate_findings.impact: Parallel or retried execution can double-apply decisions, lose evidence, or leave multiple contradictory completion receipts for one goal attempt.

explicit_non_gaps.statement: Worker authority is explicitly bounded: worker output is proposal-only, workers cannot certify global or parent completion, and unsupported content cannot become canonical or completion evidence.
The core explicitly requires coverage evidence for no-op or low-change claims and names both the material-claim fields and no-material fields/disposition reasons.
Provider neutrality and independent worker versus verifier/adjudicator settings are explicit, and the negative constraints reject both single-provider correctness and forced same-model execution.

Strong-certification failure behavior is explicit at two layers: an underqualified verifier/adjudicator prevents proceeding, and verifier/adjudicator unavailability blocks rather than completes the goal.
Validator failures and out-of-scope writes explicitly escalate even when worker confidence is high; worker confidence alone is not accepted as a completion basis.

A receipt is required for every goal outcome, worker claims are separated from runtime certification decisions, and ledger/source memory is explicitly barred from being treated as canonical product truth.

The three certification profiles enumerate concrete evidence expectations for lightweight, standard, and strong-certification goals, including replayable evidence, deterministic validation where available, changed-artifact hashes, and a written certificate for strong certification.
The policy explicitly prohibits uncapped or unredacted raw logs inside receipts and requires separate, referenced log storage while prohibiting secret retention.
GUI scope is not silently assigned to these units: every core unit is explicitly gui_related false, while cross-document implementation surfaces are named separately.
The planning/build boundary is explicit because all six core units set create_worknodes false.
Receipt ownership is explicit: Project_Output_Artifacts remains only a boundary/distinction reference and does not own Goal Runtime evidence receipts.

unknowns.statement: Exact provider-specific default tier mappings are intentionally deferred and therefore cannot be assessed in this window.
The content and contract of GRS-006 are outside the assigned ranges, so the prerequisite that GRS-009 inherits from GRS-006 is unknown here.

The detailed consumer, storage, and GUI contracts in FinalGUISpec, Models_System, Multi-Account, Runtime_Artifacts_Panel, storage-plan, and the future implementation surfaces are not visible under the blind window scope.

The behavior and fixtures of the named future verifier, escalation, model-role, receipt-tier, completion-receipt, and retention/redaction tests are unknown because only their future validation-surface names appear.
GRS-015 is visible only as after-context, so its progress-fingerprint, blocker, budget, retry, and validator rules cannot be used to resolve core ordering or termination gaps.

exact_evidence_refs.exact_quote: Goal Runtime separates worker, planner, evaluator, reducer, verifier, adjudicator, and runtime controller roles. Workers have bounded authority, and weak-worker outputs are proposal only until stronger or deterministic layers verify, merge, route, or complete them. A low quality agent over massive documents may miss a lot, hallucinate issues, or claim no issues, and must never make global completion judgment. Material worker claims carry source_spans, target_spans, and evidence_refs; no-material claims use no_material_items_found with source_span_checked and reason duplicate, nonmaterial, already_covered, or context_only. Unsupported content cannot become canonical plan content or completion evidence. Workers cannot certify global or parent completion by themselves. Risk-triggered verification escalates when worker capability, confidence, scope, evidence, or validation status is insufficient.
- Worker roles cannot unilaterally mark a goal complete.
- No-op or low-change completion claims require coverage evidence.

- Material and no-material worker claims preserve source_spans, target_spans, evidence_refs, no_material_items_found, source_span_checked, and duplicate/nonmaterial/already_covered/context_only reasons.

Goal Runtime persists separate model-role policy for worker execution and verifier/adjudicator authority. The role-policy record names worker_default, planner, evaluator, adjudicator, and verifier roles, and escalation inputs include risk_class, failure_count, task type, and provider constraints. Goal Mode must provide native goal support for users will be using other models; lower quality agent paths require stronger evidence gates/escalation and must not assume the newest/biggest/highest quality model. The verifier/adjudicator model may inherit the worker model only when the inherited model satisfies the required policy for the goal's certification tier. Low-risk goals can inherit by default; standard and strong-certification goals use policy-derived verifier/adjudicator requirements; strong-certification goals block, not merely warn, when the requirement cannot be met. Exact provider-specific default tier mappings remain deferred.
- Runtime configuration supports independent worker and verifier/adjudicator role settings.
- Role-policy records preserve worker_default, planner, evaluator, adjudicator, verifier, risk_class, failure_count, and provider constraints.
- Strong-certification goals cannot proceed with an underqualified verifier/adjudicator model.
- Provider-specific default mappings can be added later without changing the role-policy contract.

Goal Runtime escalates to a stronger verifier, second-pass worker, adjudicator, or stronger policy handling when evidence is incomplete, stale, or non-replayable; child outputs conflict; retries or blockers repeat; strong-certification surfaces are touched; destructive or governance actions are proposed; worker confidence is low; high-density slice or high-signal input produces an empty/weak result; target conflict, large deletion/replacement, or failing tests appear; writes are out of scope; validators fail; or completion claims are unsupported.
- Escalation triggers are evaluated independently of provider-specific model names.
- Validator failures and out-of-scope writes escalate even when worker confidence is high.
- High-density slices, target conflicts, large deletions/replacements, failing tests, and low-confidence worker output escalate to stronger review.

Every goal produces a Goal Completion Receipt. Completion is a runtime-certified state, not a worker-model judgment. A worker can propose completion, but the controller/evaluator/certifier decides whether the goal is complete. Required inputs must be inventoried, required work represented or dispositioned, validations run or explicitly skipped with reason, acceptance criteria satisfied, unresolved items explicit, and no required source or target areas left unaccounted for. Ledger-to-Plans completion additionally requires material ledger content represented in live Plans or intentionally captured as open questions or unresolved decisions, conflicts preserved, unsupported inventions absent, and source-to-target evidence present. Receipts separate source evidence, canonical evidence, process evidence, governance evidence, unresolved items, changed artifacts, and validator outcomes.
- Every goal has a receipt or a stopped/blocked/degraded receipt explaining why completion is not certified normally.
- Receipts distinguish worker claims from controller/evaluator/certifier decisions.
- Evidence classes are recorded without treating ledger/source memory as canonical product truth.

- Goal completion certification verifies that required inputs were inventoried, represented or dispositioned, validations ran, acceptance criteria are satisfied, unresolved items are explicit, and no required source/target areas are unaccounted for.

- Ledger-to-Plans receipts prove material ledger content in live Plans or explicit open-question/unresolved-decision disposition, conflicts preserved, unsupported inventions absent, and source-to-target evidence.

negative_constraints:
  - Do not let done be only a worker-model judgment.
  - Do not allow a worker or child goal to certify global or parent completion by itself.
  - Do not count source ledger text, scaffold, or process artifacts as canonical live Plans evidence.

Completion certification is tiered by risk and phase. Lightweight read-only or answer-only goals require final answer, addressed objective, known uncertainty, no file mutation, and no hidden blocker. Standard code/doc work requires changed files, task checklist disposition, relevant tests/checks run or skipped with reason, no known unresolved blockers, and respected user constraints. Strong-certification goals require replayable evidence, source-to-target mapping where applicable, independent verifier or verifier role, deterministic validators where available, changed artifact hashes, explicit unresolved/open items, and written completion certificate.
- File-writing, Plan-writing, code-editing, test-running, migration, destructive, and governance-sensitive goals use stronger certification than read-only goals.
- Strong-certification receipts include replayable evidence and independent/deterministic verification where available.
- Standard receipts account for checks, changed files, constraints, and blockers.

Verifier/adjudicator unavailable behavior is tiered: low-risk goals may finish with a degraded receipt; standard goals may degrade only when no mutation or required check is affected; strong-certification goals become blocked, not complete. Receipts retain hashes, summaries, changed files, command identities, validator outputs, child receipts, verifier/adjudicator decisions, and source-to-target mappings where relevant. Raw logs are capped, redacted, separately stored, and referenced by hash/path.
- Strong-certification goals do not complete when verifier/adjudicator requirements cannot be met.
- Standard degraded receipts are allowed only when mutation and required checks are unaffected.
- Raw logs are never stored uncapped or unredacted inside the receipt.

### GRS-015 - Progress Fingerprints, Budgets, And Validators

```yaml
plan_unit_id: GRS-015
unit_type: requirement
status: accepted
owner_doc: Plans/Goal_Runtime_System.md
canonical_text: >-
  Goal Runtime uses progress_fingerprint records, blocker_signature, artifact hashes, retry/blocker detection, repeat_count, no-progress continuations, hard budgets, limit statuses, and deterministic validators as first-class gates. Budget and limit gates carry exact fields max_turns, max_tokens, max_wall_time_seconds, max_parallel_agents, budget_limited, and usage_limited. Repeated identical blockers without artifact change route to repair/adjudication rather than infinite retry, and a goal cannot hide repeated non-progress, validator failure, or budget exhaustion behind a normal completion claim.
